title: Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS Is Surprisingly Rich in Methanol
summary:
Comet 3I/ATLAS is continuing to surprise astronomers. New observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in Chile reveal that this interstellar visitor contains an unusually large amount of methanol — a type of alcohol. In fact, its methanol abundance exceeds that seen in almost all known comets from our own solar system.

"Observing 3I/ATLAS is like taking a fingerprint from another solar system," says Nathan Roth, lead author and professor at American University. "The details reveal what it's made of, and it's bursting with methanol in a way we just don't usually see in comets in our own solar system."

The team used ALMA's Atacama Compact Array to observe 3I/ATLAS in late 2025 as it approached the Sun. As sunlight heated the comet's icy surface, gas and dust escaped, forming a bright coma — a cloud of gas and dust around the core. By studying the molecules in this coma, astronomers could identify the chemical makeup of the material the comet carries.

They focused on two molecules: methanol (CH3OH) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a nitrogen-bearing organic molecule common in comets. ALMA revealed methanol-to-HCN ratios of roughly 70 and 120 on two dates — placing 3I/ATLAS among the most methanol-rich comets ever studied.

The measurements suggest the ice inside 3I/ATLAS formed under, or was later exposed to, conditions very different from those in our solar system. Earlier James Webb Space Telescope observations found its coma was dominated by carbon dioxide while far from the Sun. Now, abundant methanol adds to the list of unusual features.

ALMA's high resolution also allowed astronomers to track how molecules are released. Hydrogen cyanide appears to come mostly from the comet's nucleus, which is typical. But methanol comes from both the nucleus and ice particles floating in the coma. These tiny icy grains act like miniature comets, releasing methanol as they warm up.

This is the first time researchers have traced this type of outgassing in an interstellar object. 3I/ATLAS is only the third confirmed interstellar object, after 1I/'Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov. Each one offers a rare opportunity to compare our solar system with others. As Roth puts it, this comet is "bursting with methanol in a way we just don't usually see" — and it's helping us understand how planets and comets form around distant stars.
why_it_matters: This study shows how astrochemistry lets scientists 'read' a comet from another star system. The results will help researchers understand which chemical ingredients are common across the galaxy and how unique our own solar system's building blocks might be.

background_read: Comets are leftover chunks of ice, dust, and rock from the time when planets formed.
When sunlight warms a comet, ice can turn directly into gas, creating a coma — a temporary atmosphere of gas and dust around the solid core.
3I/ATLAS is the third confirmed interstellar object (an object that came from outside our solar system), after 1I/'Oumuamua and 2I/Borisov.
ALMA (the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array) is a collection of radio telescopes in Chile that detects the faint light molecules give off, letting astronomers identify chemicals in space.
The James Webb Space Telescope, the most powerful infrared observatory in space, had already found that this same comet released carbon dioxide while it was still far from the Sun.

perspectives.description: The detection is a milestone because, for the first time, astronomers traced outgassing from both a comet's nucleus and its icy grains in an interstellar object. It gives a chemical fingerprint of material formed in another solar system.
Astronomers have observed only three interstellar objects, so the sample size is tiny. A single methanol-rich comet cannot by itself prove how typical other planetary systems are.

Every interstellar object so far has been different, and 3I/ATLAS adds another unique data point. Astronomers are still in the early stages of understanding what these visitors mean for how planets and comets form.

Future telescopes and possibly even spacecraft missions may study interstellar objects more closely. Comparing methanol-rich comets like 3I/ATLAS with our own solar system could reveal whether the chemistry needed for life is common elsewhere.
